lessonTitle: Tooling and Surface Finish: HSS, Carbide, Roughness and Cutting Fluids

blocks.text: A finishing pass on a steel shaft at a feed of 0.3 mm per revolution leaves a faint spiral pattern you can feel with a fingernail. Slowing the feed to 0.1 mm per revolution makes the surface almost smooth, at three times the machining time. The pattern is not a defect in the machine: it is the shape of the tool nose copied onto the work.

blocks.markdown: The cutting tool must be harder than the work and keep its edge at the temperatures cutting produces, which can exceed 600 degrees C at the tool tip. Two tool materials dominate workshops: **high-speed steel (HSS)** and **cemented carbide** (tungsten carbide grains bound in cobalt). Each is a trade between hardness and toughness.

rows: Very high (about 1400 to 1800 HV, harder than HSS)
Retains hardness to about 800 to 1000 degrees C
High; resists shock and interrupted cuts
Typical cutting speed in mild steel
About 150 to 250 m/min, several times higher
Cheaper; can be reground to sharp edges, drills, taps, reamers
More expensive; brazed tips or replaceable inserts
Low speeds, small shops, complex form tools, drills
High production, hard materials, rigid machines
blocks.caption: Typical values only; they depend on the grade and coating.

blocks.title: Hardness versus toughness
blocks.text: Carbide is harder and stays hard when hot, so it cuts several times faster, but it is brittle and needs a rigid set-up. HSS is tougher and cheaper, so it suits low speeds, light machines, interrupted cuts and complex shapes.

blocks.markdown: **Theoretical surface roughness.** In turning with feed $f$ (mm per revolution) the round nose of the tool leaves a series of small arcs, like a scalloped surface. The peaks lie between two adjacent tool positions a feed apart, and the valley depth depends on the nose radius $r$. For a small feed compared with the nose radius, the geometry gives the peak-to-valley height $R_t$ and the arithmetic average roughness $R_a$.

blocks.caption: Theoretical peak-to-valley height Rt and average roughness Ra for turning with feed f per revolution and tool nose radius r (all in the same length unit). Valid for small f compared with r, with a sharp, stable tool.

blocks.title: Estimating Ra
blocks.prompt: A finishing pass uses a feed $f=0.2$ mm/rev and a tool nose radius $r=0.8$ mm. Estimate the theoretical Ra.

steps.text: Substitute into $R_a\approx f^2/(32r)$ with both in mm.

blocks.answer: Theoretical Ra is about 1.56 micrometres. Halving the feed would reduce it by a factor of 4.

blocks.title: Choosing a feed for a target finish
blocks.prompt: A drawing requires $R_a\le0.8\ \mu$m on a turned diameter. The insert has nose radius $r=1.2$ mm. Find the largest feed.

steps.text: Convert Ra to mm: 0.8 micrometres is 0.0008 mm. Then 32 x 1.2 x 0.0008 = 0.03072 mm^2.
Take the square root: 0.1753 mm/rev. Choose a slightly smaller practical feed such as 0.15 mm/rev.

blocks.answer: The largest feed is about 0.175 mm/rev; the practical choice is 0.15 mm/rev.

blocks.markdown: The formula is a **best case**. Real surfaces are rougher because of tool wear, a built-up edge of work material welded to the tool, machine vibration and a dull tool. The formula shows the main levers: reduce the feed, increase the nose radius, keep the tool sharp, and reduce chatter. A larger nose radius also raises cutting forces and the tendency to chatter on flexible work.

**Cutting fluids.** Most of the energy in cutting becomes heat at the tool tip, and the tool wears faster as it gets hotter. A cutting fluid does three jobs: it **cools** the work and tool, **lubricates** the tool-chip and tool-work interfaces (reducing friction, heat and built-up edge), and **flushes chips** from the cut. Typical fluids are water-based emulsions, which cool best, and oils, which lubricate best.

items: Lower temperature: slows thermal wear, so tool life increases and a higher speed becomes possible.
Lower friction: reduces cutting force and heat generation, and reduces the built-up edge.
Better surface finish: less built-up edge and smaller thermal distortion of the work.
Chip clearance: swarf is washed out of the cut and does not scratch the surface.
Corrosion protection of machine and work.

blocks.title: Thermal shock and handling
blocks.text: Intermittent flood coolant on a hot carbide milling insert can cause thermal cracking, so some carbide milling is run dry or with a mist. Cutting fluids also need correct handling and disposal: skin contact, mist inhalation and bacterial growth are hazards, so they must be controlled.

points: HSS is tough, cheaper and cuts at low speeds; carbide is harder, retains hardness when hot and cuts several times faster but is more brittle.
Theoretical roughness in turning is Ra = f squared over 32 r, so it falls with the square of the feed and in proportion to the nose radius; real surfaces are rougher.
Cutting fluids cool, lubricate and flush chips, increasing tool life and improving finish.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly compares cemented carbide with HSS as a tool material?

options.text: Carbide is harder and keeps its hardness at higher temperatures, but is less tough
Carbide is tougher and softens at a lower temperature
Carbide and HSS have the same hot hardness
Carbide is cheaper and easier to regrind

questions.correctOptionText: Carbide is harder and keeps its hardness at higher temperatures, but is less tough

distractorRationale.b: Carbide is more brittle than HSS and retains hardness to higher temperature.
distractorRationale.c: Carbide keeps hardness to a much higher temperature than HSS.
distractorRationale.d: Carbide is more expensive and is not reground like HSS.

questions.explanation: Carbide has higher hardness and hot hardness, which allows higher cutting speeds, but its brittleness makes it less suited to shock. HSS is the tougher, cheaper material.

questions.stem: A small workshop machines a variety of one-off parts on a light, older lathe, with many interrupted cuts and a need for specially ground form tools. Which tool material is the better choice?

options.text: High-speed steel
Cemented carbide at 250 m/min
A ceramic insert
Carbide with no coolant

distractorRationale.b: Carbide at that speed needs a rigid, powerful machine and fails under shock.
distractorRationale.c: Ceramic inserts are even more brittle and need rigid machines.
distractorRationale.d: The problem is toughness and machine capability, not coolant.

questions.explanation: Light machines and interrupted cuts favour the tough material, and HSS is easy to grind into form tools. The high speeds that suit carbide are not available on the older lathe.

questions.stem: Which pair of functions do cutting fluids mainly perform in machining steel?

options.text: Cooling and lubricating the cutting zone, and flushing chips
Increasing the hardness of the work and the tool
Heating the work to soften it
Eliminating the need for sharp tools

questions.correctOptionText: Cooling and lubricating the cutting zone, and flushing chips

distractorRationale.b: Fluids do not harden the work or the tool.
distractorRationale.c: Fluids remove heat; they do not soften the work by heating it.
distractorRationale.d: A sharp tool is still needed.

questions.explanation: Cutting fluid takes heat away, reduces friction at the tool contact surfaces and washes chips from the cut. These effects lower tool temperature, extend tool life and improve the surface.

questions.stem: Why might a carbide face-milling insert in an interrupted cut be run dry instead of with flood coolant?

options.text: Alternate heating and cooling can cause thermal cracks in the brittle insert
Carbide cannot be wetted by liquids
The coolant would dissolve the work
Dry cutting always gives the best finish

questions.correctOptionText: Alternate heating and cooling can cause thermal cracks in the brittle insert

distractorRationale.b: Carbide can be wetted; the problem is thermal shock.
distractorRationale.c: The coolant does not dissolve steel.
distractorRationale.d: Dry cutting is not always best; it is a trade-off.

questions.explanation: In an interrupted cut the insert heats during cutting and cools between cuts, and flood coolant makes the temperature swings larger. The brittle carbide can crack from the thermal shock.

questions.stem: In turning, the feed is doubled with all else unchanged. What happens to the theoretical Ra?

options.text: It increases by a factor of 4
It doubles
It halves
It does not change

questions.correctOptionText: It increases by a factor of 4

distractorRationale.b: Ra is proportional to the square of the feed, not the feed.
distractorRationale.d: The feed is the main variable in the formula.

questions.explanation: Since $R_a\approx f^2/(32r)$, doubling the feed multiplies the roughness by $2^2=4$. This is why halving the feed in a finishing pass reduces Ra by a factor of 4.

questions.stem: A turned surface is made with a feed of 0.12 mm/rev and a tool nose radius of 0.4 mm. Estimate the theoretical Ra in micrometres.
questions.explanation: Using $R_a=f^2/(32r)=0.12^2/(32\times0.4)=1.125\times10^{-3}$ mm. This is 1.125 micrometres, the best case with a sharp, stable tool.

questions.stem: A finishing pass must achieve Ra of at most 0.8 micrometres using a tool with nose radius 1.2 mm. What is the largest feed, in mm/rev?
questions.explanation: Rearranging, $f=\sqrt{32rR_a}=\sqrt{32\times1.2\times0.0008}=0.175$ mm/rev. A slightly smaller practical feed gives a safety margin.

questions.stem: A part is turned at a feed of 0.25 mm/rev and must have a theoretical Ra no greater than 1.6 micrometres. What minimum tool nose radius, in mm, is needed?
questions.explanation: From $R_a=f^2/(32r)$, $r=f^2/(32R_a)=0.0625/(32\times0.0016)=1.22$ mm. A larger radius lowers the roughness for the same feed, but raises the cutting forces.

questions.stem: Compare high-speed steel and carbide cutting tools in hardness, toughness, cutting speed and cost, and state how cutting fluid is used with each.
markingGuide: HSS: tough, lower hot hardness (softens around 600 degrees C), lower speeds, cheaper, can be reground
Carbide: harder, retains hardness to higher temperature, higher speeds, brittle, more expensive
Both are matched to the machine and job, such as interrupted cuts and rigidity
Cutting fluid cools and lubricates, increasing tool life for both
Mention of flood coolant for HSS and caution with carbide in interrupted cuts because of thermal shock
questions.explanation: The answer should link each material's properties to the way it is used. Cutting fluid is more routinely used with HSS, while carbide may be run dry or with controlled cooling to avoid thermal shock.

questions.stem: Explain why a turned surface has a theoretical roughness that depends on feed and nose radius, why real surfaces are rougher, and list three ways to improve the surface finish.
markingGuide: Tool nose leaves scallops between adjacent feed positions
Height depends on feed squared and inversely on nose radius
Real surfaces are worse due to built-up edge, vibration and tool wear
Improve finish by reducing feed, increasing nose radius, using a sharp tool or reducing vibration
Cutting fluid reduces built-up edge and improves finish
questions.explanation: The scalloped profile follows from the geometry of the nose and feed, giving Ra proportional to f squared over r. Real effects such as built-up edge, wear and chatter add to the roughness and can be reduced by tool and process changes.
